Can a squatter take ownership of a house in Washington?

Only by meeting the adverse possession statutes for a long stretch of time. The law sets a limitation period on the owner's right to sue and two statutes that let a long-term occupant become the legal owner under defined conditions.

For owners, the practical point is timing. The sections below separate an adverse possession claim from a trespass or unlawful detainer problem.

How long does adverse possession take in Washington?

The general limit is ten years, and one route is shortened to seven years when the occupant has paper title and pays the taxes. Three statutes carry the rules:

  • RCW 4.16.020 sets ten years for actions to recover real property or its possession. An owner cannot maintain the action unless the owner or a predecessor or grantor was seized or possessed of the premises within ten years before the suit.
  • RCW 7.28.050 covers a person in actual, open and notorious possession for seven successive years who has a connected title in law or equity deducible of record. The owner's action must be brought within seven years after possession was taken, or from the time the possessor acquires title if that comes later.
  • RCW 7.28.070 covers a person in actual, open and notorious possession under claim and color of title made in good faith, who stays seven successive years and pays all taxes legally assessed on the land during that time. That person is held to be the legal owner to the extent of the paper title.

The words that recur are actual, open and notorious, and successive. Whether an occupant's facts fit those words is a question for a court, so an owner who suspects a claim should talk to a Washington attorney early.

Which situations are protected from adverse possession in Washington?

Public land and land held by certain owners with a legal disability are carved out. RCW 7.28.090 says the claim and color of title statutes do not extend to lands of the United States or this state, school lands, or lands held for any public purpose. They also do not extend to land where the holder of the adverse title is under eighteen, or has been placed under a guardianship or conservatorship. That person must bring an action to recover the land within three years after the disability ends.

RuleTimeKey condition
RCW 4.16.020(1)10 yearsLimit on actions to recover real property or possession
RCW 7.28.0507 yearsActual, open and notorious possession with connected title deducible of record
RCW 7.28.0707 yearsClaim and color of title in good faith, plus payment of all taxes assessed
RCW 7.28.0903 years after disability endsOwner who is a minor or under guardianship or conservatorship

Source: Revised Code of Washington (app.leg.wa.gov).

What happens when someone files an adverse possession claim?

These disputes are heard in superior court, including through an action to quiet title. Under RCW 7.28.010, a person with a valid subsisting interest in real property and a right to possession may recover it by action in the superior court of the proper county against the tenant in possession, and may seek a judgment quieting or removing a cloud from the title. A person in actual possession can also bring a quiet title action against unknown heirs of someone known to be dead.

RCW 7.28.083 adds money consequences for actions filed on or after July 1, 2012. A party who prevails against the record title holder, or a later purchaser from that holder, may be required to:

  • Reimburse part or all of the taxes and assessments the record holder paid during the possession, if proven by competent evidence.
  • Pay the county treasurer part or all of taxes levied after the claim was filed that remain unpaid when judgment is entered.

The court divides taxes between the land acquired and the land the titleholder keeps, as appears equitable and just. The prevailing party may also ask the court for costs and reasonable attorney fees, which the court may award in whole or part. Both sides therefore carry real cost risk once a claim reaches court.

How can an owner remove someone who has no right to be on the property?

Washington uses the unlawful detainer statutes in chapter 59.12 RCW, and for a person who entered without permission the notice period is short. RCW 59.12.030(6) reaches a person who, without the owner's permission and without color of title, enters land of another and fails or refuses to leave after three days' written notice served in the manner the statute requires. That person may also face criminal charges under chapter 9A.52 RCW.

Forcible detainer is a separate offense under RCW 59.12.020. It covers holding property by force or by menaces and threats of violence. It also covers entering at night or while the occupant is away and then refusing for three days after demand to give the property back to the former occupant. The statute defines the occupant as someone who was in peaceable and undisturbed possession for the five days before the unlawful entry.

Once an unlawful detainer case is filed, RCW 59.12.090 lets the plaintiff apply for a writ of restitution restoring the property. The superior court clerk issues it, and it is returnable in twenty days. If the plaintiff asks for it before judgment, a bond is required, set by the court, to cover costs and damages if the writ turns out to have been wrongly obtained. Ask a Washington attorney or the superior court clerk about the papers needed in your county.

What criminal trespass charges can apply in Washington?

Two degrees of criminal trespass can apply to someone who stays without right. Criminal trespass in the first degree, RCW 9A.52.070, is knowingly entering or remaining unlawfully in a building, and it is a gross misdemeanor. Criminal trespass in the second degree, RCW 9A.52.080, covers knowingly entering or remaining unlawfully in or upon premises of another in circumstances that do not amount to first degree, and it is a misdemeanor.

Whether police or a prosecutor will act depends on the facts, including whether the person claims permission, a lease or an ownership interest.

What should a Washington owner do about an occupied house they want to sell?

Deal with the occupancy question first, then sell. Keep records of when you last visited, who has keys, and what notices you have sent, because dates matter for every statute above. Check the tax records with the county treasurer, since payment of taxes is an element of a claim under RCW 7.28.070.

If the house is vacant, inherited, or has an occupant you cannot move, a cash buyer can look at it as is and explain what a closing will need. Bring copies of any notices, court filings and writ so the closing agent can see where things stand.

Frequently asked questions

How long must someone live in a house before claiming it in Washington?

The general statute of limitations for recovering real property is ten years (RCW 4.16.020). Seven years can apply when the occupant has color of title in good faith and pays all the taxes (RCW 7.28.070), or has a connected record title (RCW 7.28.050).

Do squatters have to pay property taxes to win in Washington?

Under RCW 7.28.070, the occupant must pay all taxes legally assessed during the seven years. Under RCW 7.28.083, a court may also order a winning claimant to reimburse the record owner for taxes paid or pay unpaid taxes to the county treasurer.

How much notice does a trespasser get before an unlawful detainer case in Washington?

For a person who entered without permission and without color of title, RCW 59.12.030(6) provides three days' written notice served as the statute requires. If the person does not leave, the owner can file an unlawful detainer action in superior court.

Is trespassing a crime in Washington?

Yes. Knowingly entering or remaining unlawfully in a building is first degree criminal trespass, a gross misdemeanor. Doing so on other premises is second degree, a misdemeanor (RCW 9A.52.070 and 9A.52.080).

Can a squatter claim public land in Washington?

No under the claim and color of title statutes. RCW 7.28.090 says they do not extend to land of the United States or this state, school lands, or lands held for any public purpose.

Washington Landlord Tenant Law and Tenant Rights: Rules for Selling a Rental

Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Washington?

Can a Washington landlord end a tenancy to sell the house?

Only for a single-family residence, and only with at least 90 days' advance written notice. RCW 59.18.650 bars a Washington landlord from evicting, refusing to continue a tenancy or ending a periodic tenancy except for the causes the statute lists. One listed cause is that the owner elects to sell a single-family residence.

The statute defines "elects to sell" as making reasonable attempts to sell within 30 days after the tenant leaves, at a minimum by listing the home at a reasonable price with a realty agency or on the real estate multiple listing service. Two facts create a rebuttable presumption that the owner never meant to sell: no listing within 30 days of the tenant moving out, or, within 90 days after the move-out or the listing date, whichever is later, the owner pulls the unit off the market, rents it to someone else or otherwise signals no intent to sell.

A landlord who wants to sell a duplex or a unit in a larger building should read the other listed causes and check with an attorney, because the sale ground is written for single-family homes.

What happens to a lease when a rental house is sold?

A landlord may end a Washington tenancy only for a cause listed in RCW 59.18.650, so the lease terms and that list decide what a buyer takes on. A tenant in a fixed-term lease stays through the term unless the landlord and tenant agree in writing to end it early and the tenant gets at least 60 days to move, per subsection (5) of that section.

For the buyer, that means the house may come with a tenant already in place. Three routes fit the statute:

  • Sell the property subject to the existing lease and rent.
  • Serve the 90-day notice for the sale of a single-family residence and list the home once the tenant has moved.
  • Reach a written mutual agreement with the tenant to end the tenancy early.

Every written notice under the cause list must be served as RCW 59.12.040 describes and must describe the facts supporting the cause with enough detail for the tenant to respond.

What does a landlord owe the tenant's deposit on a sale?

The deposit has to follow the tenancy. RCW 59.18.270 requires a landlord to deposit a security deposit promptly in a trust account at a Washington financial institution or licensed escrow agent, give the tenant a written receipt, and tell the tenant in writing where the money is held. If the landlord's status transfers to someone else during the tenancy, the funds move at the same moment to an equivalent trust account of the successor landlord, who must promptly notify the tenant of the new depository.

The statute adds a rule for foreclosures. If the home is foreclosed on and the deposit is not passed to the successor, the former owner must promptly refund the full deposit to the tenant, or face damages up to two times the deposit. The tenant's claim to deposit money also ranks ahead of the landlord's creditors, even where the money was mixed with other funds.

A seller of a tenant-occupied house should list the deposit amount in the purchase contract and confirm in writing who is responsible for it at closing.

When must a landlord return a security deposit in Washington?

Within 30 days after the tenancy ends and the tenant has moved out. RCW 59.18.280 requires a full and specific statement of why any part of the deposit is kept, with copies of estimates or paid invoices backing up damage charges, plus any refund due. The 30 days run from the date the landlord learns of an abandonment if the tenant simply left. Delivering the papers personally or mailing them first class within the 30 days satisfies the rule.

A landlord may not keep deposit money for:

  • wear from ordinary use of the home;
  • carpet cleaning, unless the landlord documents wear beyond ordinary use;
  • repair or replacement of fixtures and appliances whose condition was not recorded on the move-in checklist;
  • more than the cost of repairing the damaged part, when only part of an item is damaged.

Miss the deadline and the landlord owes the full deposit and cannot raise claims against it. A court may award up to two times the deposit for an intentional refusal, and the winner in a deposit lawsuit recovers costs and reasonable attorneys' fees.

How much notice must a landlord give to show the house to buyers?

One day's notice is enough to show a rental to prospective or actual purchasers, while other entries need two days. RCW 59.18.150 says that, except in an emergency or when it is impracticable, a landlord must give at least two days' written notice of intent to enter and may enter only at reasonable times. The notice must give the exact date and time, or the earliest and latest possible times, and a phone number for the tenant to object or reschedule.

Where the visit is to exhibit the unit to buyers or tenants, the tenant may not unreasonably withhold consent if the landlord gave at least one day's notice. The landlord also may not excessively exhibit the unit or use entry to harass the tenant.

A landlord or tenant who keeps breaking these rules after one written good-faith notice that lists the date and time of the violation can be liable for up to $100 per violation. The prevailing party may recover costs and attorneys' fees, so keep every notice in writing.

How much notice does a rent increase or a tenant's move-out require?

A rent increase needs at least 90 days' prior written notice to each affected tenant, and it cannot take effect before the rental agreement term ends, under RCW 59.18.140(3). Subsidized tenancies where rent depends on household income need only 30 days. A transitional rule applies to some fixed-term leases signed or renewed before May 7, 2025, that had more than 60 but fewer than 90 days left on that date: 60 days' notice.

A tenant ending a month-to-month tenancy gives written notice of 20 days or more before the end of a rental period, per RCW 59.18.200(1). A member of the armed forces, or that member's spouse or dependent, may leave on shorter notice when permanent change of station or deployment orders do not allow 20 days.

Landlords planning to demolish, substantially rehabilitate or change the use of a building owe tenants a 120-day written notice under the same section, which matters to an owner thinking about redevelopment before a sale.

What is the penalty for removing a tenant illegally in Washington?

A landlord who removes a tenant, or causes removal, in violation of RCW 59.18.650 is liable for wrongful eviction. The tenant who wins is entitled to the greater of economic and noneconomic damages or three times the monthly rent, plus reasonable attorneys' fees and court costs.

That penalty makes a clean paper trail important for any seller with a tenant. Keep copies of written notices, proof of how they were served, the listing date and the deposit accounting. If you are unsure which cause applies, ask the superior court clerk for the unlawful detainer forms, or hire a Washington landlord-tenant attorney before you serve anything.

Key notice periods in one place

SituationNotice or deadline
Owner elects to sell a single-family home90 days' written notice
Rent increase90 days (30 days for income-based subsidized tenancies)
Tenant ends month-to-month tenancy20 days or more, in writing
Entry to show to buyersOne day's notice
Deposit statement and refund30 days after move-out

Frequently asked questions

Does a new owner have to honor an existing Washington lease?

A landlord may end a tenancy only for a cause listed in RCW 59.18.650, and the sale of a single-family residence is one of them, with 90 days' written notice. The deposit trust money must transfer to a successor landlord under RCW 59.18.270.

How much notice must a Washington landlord give before showing a rental house to a buyer?

One day. RCW 59.18.150(6) says a tenant may not unreasonably refuse entry to exhibit the unit to purchasers when the landlord gave at least one day's notice, though other entries need two days' written notice.

Can a landlord raise rent on a tenant before selling?

Only with at least 90 days' prior written notice, and not before the rental agreement term ends. Subsidized income-based tenancies need 30 days under RCW 59.18.140(3).

Who is responsible for the tenant's deposit when the house is sold?

The deposit moves with the tenancy. RCW 59.18.270 requires the funds to transfer to the successor landlord's trust account at the same time, and the successor must promptly tell the tenant where the money is held.

What can a tenant recover if a landlord evicts without a valid cause?

The greater of economic and noneconomic damages or three times the monthly rent, plus reasonable attorneys' fees and court costs, under RCW 59.18.650(4).

title: Washington Eviction Notice Rules: Notice Types, Days and Selling the House
content:
Washington Eviction Notice Rules: Notice Types, Days and Selling the House

Selling in Washington?

How many days of notice does a Washington landlord have to give before an eviction?

It depends on the reason. For unpaid rent on a residential tenancy, the landlord must serve a written notice to pay or vacate and wait 14 days. For a lease violation other than rent, the wait is 10 days. For waste, a nuisance or an unlawful business, it is three days. These periods come from RCW 59.12.030, and the residential cause list in RCW 59.18.650 ties to them.

A tenant becomes liable for unlawful detainer on a rent or lease default only after the notice has gone unanswered for the full period, so the notice comes before any court filing.

What are the main Washington eviction notice types and periods?

With narrow exceptions for certain fixed-term leases, a Washington residential landlord cannot end a tenancy without one of the causes written in RCW 59.18.650. The table lists the notice lengths that matter most to an owner who is trying to sell.

ReasonWritten notice
Unpaid rent14 days to pay or vacate
Lease or rule violation other than rent10 days to fix it or vacate
Waste, nuisance or unlawful activity3 days to quit
Owner or family moving in90 days
Owner selling a single-family home90 days
Home certified or condemned as unfit to live in30 days
Tenant shares a kitchen or bath with the owner20 days
Demolition, major rehab or change of use120 days

What must a Washington 14-day pay or vacate notice say?

RCW 59.18.057 prescribes a form that must be used substantially as written. It lists unpaid rent, utilities and other recurring charges by month, shows a total amount due, and says where the money is to be paid. It also tells the tenant that payment must follow the rental agreement or be made by nonelectronic means such as a cashier's check or money order.

The notice must tell the tenant that any payment is applied first to the total on the notice. It must also describe resources: the Attorney General's website for rental help, the Eviction Defense Screening Line for qualifying low-income renters, the Northwest Justice Project CLEAR hotline, dispute resolution centers for low-cost mediation, and the right to an interpreter in court.

  • List each month and each category separately.
  • Give a payment address and the owner or landlord name.
  • Date the notice so the days can be counted from service.

How does a landlord serve an eviction notice in Washington?

RCW 59.12.040 allows three ways to serve. The first is handing a copy to the tenant in person. If the tenant is absent from the home, a copy can be left with a person of suitable age and discretion there, and a second copy is mailed to the tenant's residence. If the residence is not known or nobody suitable can be found, the landlord can post the notice in a conspicuous place on the property, give a copy to anyone living there, and mail a copy.

When service is by mail, it is complete on the day the copy goes into the mail from within Washington with postage paid, but five more days must pass before an action can be started on that notice. Any termination notice must also state the date by which the tenant has to vacate or, where it applies, comply.

The causes listed in RCW 59.18.650 require more. A notice under that section must be served the same way and must describe the facts known to the landlord at that time with enough detail for the tenant to prepare a response.

Can a Washington landlord end a tenancy because the house is being sold?

Yes, but only on the terms in RCW 59.18.650(2)(e). A tenant who stays after the owner elects to sell a single-family residence can be removed if the landlord gave at least 90 days' advance written notice of the date possession is to end. The owner is treated as electing to sell when the owner makes reasonable attempts within 30 days after the tenant leaves, and at a minimum lists the home at a reasonable price with a realty agency or on the multiple listing service.

There is a rebuttable presumption that the owner did not intend to sell if the home is not listed within 30 days of the tenant moving out. The same presumption applies if, within 90 days of the move-out or the listing date, whichever is later, the owner pulls the house off the market, rents it to someone else, or otherwise shows no intent to sell.

A fixed-term lease cannot be ended early on this ground. Subsection (5) says an owner may do that only with the tenant's written consent and at least 60 days for the tenant to vacate.

What happens if a landlord removes a tenant without following the rules?

A landlord who removes a tenant in violation of RCW 59.18.650 is liable for wrongful eviction. The tenant who wins can recover the greater of their economic and noneconomic damages or three times the monthly rent, plus reasonable attorneys' fees and court costs. The exposure applies to any removal that breaks the section, so an owner who wants a vacant house for sale should follow the notice and court steps.

Washington also provides that an indigent tenant in an eviction case may have a court-appointed attorney, subject to available funding, according to the Attorney General's landlord-tenant page.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Washington houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

What should a Washington owner do next if a tenant will not leave a house that is for sale?

Count the notice period from the service date, keep proof of how the notice was delivered, and do not file anything in superior court before the period runs out. Unlawful detainer for unpaid rent applies when the tenant neither pays nor leaves within the notice period. Lease violations can be cured within 10 days of service.

When you are weighing a sale, add up the timeline. A 90-day sale notice has to come first, and a court case follows if the tenant stays. A written move-out agreement is another path: for a fixed-term lease the statute allows an early end when the tenant consents in writing and gets at least 60 days to leave. A lawyer or the county superior court clerk can confirm local filing steps.

Frequently asked questions

How long is a Washington eviction notice for unpaid rent?

It is 14 days for a residential tenancy. The landlord serves a written pay-or-vacate notice, and if the tenant does not pay or leave within 14 days after service, the landlord may file an unlawful detainer case.

Can a Washington landlord evict without a reason?

Generally no. RCW 59.18.650 says a landlord may not evict, refuse to continue a tenancy or end a periodic tenancy except for listed causes. Narrow exceptions let a landlord end certain leases of six months or longer at their end with 60 days' written notice.

How much notice does a Washington landlord give to sell the house?

At least 90 days' written notice for a single-family residence, and the owner must follow through by listing the home within 30 days after the tenant moves out. Otherwise there is a presumption that the owner never meant to sell.

How must a Washington eviction notice be delivered?

By personal delivery, by leaving a copy with a suitable person and mailing another, or, when neither is possible, by posting it on the property, giving a copy to a resident and mailing a copy. Mail service adds five days before a case can start.

What is the penalty for an illegal eviction in Washington?

A tenant who wins can recover the greater of actual damages or three times the monthly rent, plus attorneys' fees and court costs, under RCW 59.18.650(4).
